R1.title: The 50/30/20 rule
R1.vo: Here's the simplest budget in America: the 50/30/20 rule. Take your take-home pay. Fifty percent goes to needs — rent, groceries, utilities, minimum debt payments. Thirty percent goes to wants — eating out, subscriptions, fun. Twenty percent goes to your future — savings, investing, extra debt payoff. That's it. If 50% barely covers your needs, don't quit — shrink the gap first, then work toward the split. Save this for payday. For educational purposes only. Not financial advice.

R2.title: Waive a bank fee
R2.vo: If your bank or credit card charged you a late fee, try this. Call the number on the back of your card and say: 'I've been a customer for two years, this is my first late fee — can you waive it as a courtesy?' Keep your tone calm. Most representatives can waive one fee per year, but they won't offer unless you ask. Do this once, not every month. And never miss a payment on purpose. R3.title: Credit utilization timing
R3.vo: Credit utilization is about 30% of your FICO score. Here's the part most people miss: card companies report your balance on your statement date, not your due date. So if you spend nine hundred on a thousand-dollar limit and pay it off before the due date, it can still look like you owe ninety percent. The fix: pay most of the balance BEFORE the statement closes, then pay the rest by the due date. Aim under 30% — under 10% is even better. Check your statement date in your app. For educational purposes only. Not financial advice.

R4.title: Emergency fund ladder
R4.vo: Don't let anyone tell you that you need six months of savings before you start. Start with a starter fund: one thousand dollars. That covers a flat tire or a surprise copay. Then build one month of essential expenses — rent, food, utilities, insurance. Only after that, go for three to six months. Keep it in a high-yield savings account, not your checking account, so it's there when you need it but not easy to spend. Comment your number — where are you right now? For educational purposes only. R5.title: 401k match
R5.vo: If your employer offers a 401k match and you're not taking it, you're leaving part of your salary behind. A common match is fifty cents on the dollar up to six percent of your pay. Contribute at least enough to get the full match before you invest anywhere else. Then increase by one percent every raise — you'll barely feel it. Two things to know: vesting schedules can be different, and the market goes up and down. For educational purposes only. Not financial advice.

R6.title: Subscription audit
R6.vo: Open your phone settings, then subscriptions. Most people find at least three charges they don't use. Cancel anything you haven't opened in thirty days. Then keep a pause list — services you might want later, like after a free trial. Do this audit on the first of every month and it takes two minutes. Two minutes, maybe forty dollars a month back. R7.title: Snowball vs avalanche
R7.vo: Two ways to attack debt. Snowball: pay the smallest balance first — you get quick wins and stay motivated. Avalanche: pay the highest interest rate first — you pay less total interest. Mathematically, avalanche wins. Psychologically, snowball keeps people going. The best method is the one you won't quit. If you're disciplined, go avalanche. If you need momentum, go snowball. Either way, keep minimum payments on everything else. For educational purposes only. Not financial advice.

R8.title: 26-week savings challenge
R8.vo: Here's a savings challenge that doesn't feel crazy. Twenty-six weeks, fifty dollars a week. That's one thousand three hundred dollars — before any interest. Put it in a separate high-yield savings account and automate the transfer on payday. If fifty is too much, start at twenty-five and you still get six hundred fifty. The trick isn't the amount. It's that you never see the money. For educational purposes only. Not financial advice.

R9.title: Why your score dropped
R9.vo: Three reasons your credit score can drop even when you pay on time. One: your balance went up before your statement closed. Two: you opened a new card — the hard inquiry and lower average age can hurt for a while. Three: a collections account showed up, sometimes from a medical bill you didn't know about. Pull your free reports, dispute anything wrong, and don't panic over a few points. For educational purposes only. Not financial advice.

R10.title: The latte myth
R10.vo: You've heard: skip the latte and you'll be rich. Here's the truth. Cutting a five-dollar coffee every day saves about eighteen hundred a year — good, but it won't fix a four-thousand-dollar rent gap. Big wins come from the big three: housing, transportation, and insurance. Refinance the car, shop insurance quotes, get a roommate. Then enjoy the coffee. Small cuts help, but focus where the money actually goes. For educational purposes only. Not financial advice.

R11.title: Sinking funds
R11.vo: A sinking fund is just a savings bucket for a known expense. Christmas, car repairs, annual insurance, school supplies — you know they're coming, so stop acting surprised. Pick four categories, divide the yearly cost by twelve, and move that amount every payday. When the bill hits, you pay from the bucket, not from your groceries. No credit card, no panic. R12.title: The BNPL trap
R12.vo: Buy now, pay later feels harmless — four payments, no interest. But here's what people miss: it's easy to stack several orders and lose track, late fees add up fast, and some lenders report to credit bureaus. Also, you're spending money you haven't earned yet. Rule of thumb: if you can't pay it in full today, you probably can't afford it in four chunks. For educational purposes only. Not financial advice.

R13.title: True hourly wage
R13.vo: Your salary isn't what you think it is. Take your weekly pay, then subtract the costs of working — commute, lunches, daycare, uniforms. Divide what's left by every hour you actually give to work, including the commute. That's your real hourly wage. A fifteen dollar job with an hour commute and paid parking might really be eleven. Before you take a raise or a second job, know the number. For educational purposes only. Not financial advice.

R14.title: Credit freeze
R14.vo: A credit freeze is free and it stops someone from opening accounts in your name. Do it with all three bureaus — Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. You'll get a PIN for each one, so save them somewhere safe. It doesn't lower your score, and it doesn't stop accounts you already have. When you need new credit, unfreeze it temporarily. Ten minutes today can prevent months of cleanup. For educational purposes only. Not financial advice.

R15.title: Tax refund plan
R15.vo: A tax refund feels like a bonus, but it's your own money coming back. Before it lands, decide the split. First, cover anything you put off — a car repair, a medical bill. Second, add to your starter savings. Third, attack the highest interest debt. Whatever's left can be a small treat. Decide now, because money sitting in checking has a way of disappearing. R16.title: Medical bill check
R16.vo: Got a medical bill that makes no sense? Ask for an itemized statement. Compare it with the explanation of benefits from your insurer. Then call the billing office and ask two questions: can this be adjusted, and do you have a financial assistance policy? Many hospitals do. Never ignore it — unpaid medical bills can end up in collections. For educational purposes only. Not financial advice.

R17.title: Rent increase
R17.vo: Your lease is up and the landlord wants more. Before you panic, check three things: comparable rents in your zip code, whether you've been a reliable tenant, and if new tenants are getting a move-in special. Then ask politely for a smaller increase or a longer lease. Get the answer in writing. Worst case, you finally know your options. For educational purposes only. Not financial advice.

R18.title: Insurance quotes
R18.vo: Shopping insurance once a year can free up real cash. Get quotes for auto and renters from at least three companies. Ask about bundling and loyalty discounts — but don't assume they're automatic. Raise your deductible only if you actually have that amount saved. Cheaper isn't better if you can't cover the claim yourself. For educational purposes only. Not financial advice.

R19.title: Payday checklist
R19.vo: Payday checklist in thirty seconds. One: pay yourself first. Two: fund your sinking buckets. Three: pay the statement balance in full. Four: check for new subscriptions. Five: write down one money win. That's the whole system. Do it in the same order every time and it stops being a chore. For educational purposes only. Not financial advice.

R20.title: Weekly money date
R20.vo: Pick one day a week for twenty minutes. Open your accounts, check what came in and what went out, look at next week's bills, and write down one thing that went well. That's it. No perfect spreadsheet required. The goal isn't to obsess — it's to stop being surprised. For educational purposes only. Not financial advice.
